rows.notes: Fullest, most operational document of the three. Problem section carries specific, weighted evidence (3-4hr rebuild, two double-booking incidents, 12% reassignment rate, swaps that never reach the record) and is longer/more developed than the Solution overview. Target user is a named individual in a named situation. Success metrics section is the strongest of the set: named primary, named guardrail, and an explicit measurement window (4 weeks into peak vs. 4 weeks prior) - the only document with all three. UX section covers empty/error/edge-case states (loading state absent). FR table carries MoSCoW priority on every row; dependencies table names owner+status. Open questions has one row but it has a real owner and a milestone-based date. Weaknesses: goals are a mix of true outcomes and feature-shaped statements ('enforce the rule,' 'push changes' read as mechanisms, not outcomes); the long-haul non-goal is a one-line, undisciplined-but-acceptable mention of a distractor fact (brief scoping statement, not elaborated); and the document's voice is uniformly declarative throughout - it states conclusions ('this is a build, not a buy') without marking which calls were the author's own judgment versus a directive received, so a reader can't reliably separate decision from input. Risks table does carry an explicit stop condition tied to the primary metric at mid-peak, which is the strongest held-out showing among the three. All 5 probes answerable directly and confidently from the document alone, including a clearly assigned owner for the rest-day rule (regional ops managers, named twice).

Strongest analytical rigor of the three but weakest on the concrete deliverable the brief asked for. Problem section is excellent - richest evidence of any artifact, and explicitly names two distinct, non-overlapping failure modes rather than blurring them. Has a dedicated 'What we're told vs. what we're concluding' section that is the clearest decision-vs-input separation in the set, and an explicit, well-formed stop condition tied to both the delay metric and the rest-day rule. Risk section explicitly ranks DriverGo integration as the single highest-risk dependency ahead of the HR feed, which is more decisive than Artifact A's un-ranked pairing. However: there is no functional requirements list, no priority markers, and no UX/error/empty-state coverage at all - a real gap against the brief's explicit ask that 'design can start sketching' and 'engineering can size it... without coming back to ask.' The Risks section explicitly defers sizing ('integration spikes before we commit a ship date'), which is honest but means the document itself admits it isn't yet scopable without further work. Success criteria lack a stated measurement window. The rest-day-rule ownership question is raised but explicitly left unconfirmed ('we don't yet know who signs off... needs to be confirmed') - naming a candidate while declining to assign it means a reader can't answer that probe with confidence, so it's scored as not answered; this is the one probe this document misses. One unsourced elaboration is worth flagging on its own terms: the long-haul exclusion is stated correctly but padded with an invented detail not in the brief ('separate infrastructure with different constraints') - a minor but notable lapse in an evaluation whose central axis is evidence discipline, in contrast to Artifact A's terser, undecorated one-line version of the same exclusion.

Unfilled template shell - the title placeholder ({{title}}) is not even substituted. Every section is generic filler with zero facts from the scenario: no driver counts, no hub counts, no named scheduler, no DriverGo, no union rest-day rule, no HR certification detail, no VP commitment, no measurement figures, no stop condition, no named owners anywhere. Goals, requirements, risks, and metrics are all vague placeholder prose ('the system will support the core capability needed,' 'appropriate tracking will be put in place') that could apply to literally any initiative. None of the five probes can be answered from this document; nothing in it distinguishes this effort from any other, so scope, ownership, risk-ranking, and stop-condition questions all come back empty.

Genuinely strong, non-template-shaped PRD. Problem section is the best-evidenced of the three (Renata Okafor by name, 3-4hr rebuild, two double-booking incidents, 12% reassignment rate, the separate shift-swap-drift failure mode called out as distinct from the rebuild-speed problem) and clearly outweighs everything else in the doc. Target user is a named, situated persona, not 'all users.' Held-out criteria are where this document is unusually good for a PRD: it has a dedicated 'What we're told vs. what we're concluding' section that explicitly separates stakeholder input from authored judgment (the build-vs-buy call on the prior failed SaaS purchase is the clearest example), an explicit Stop condition section tied to the named metric and the rest-day compliance rule, and no internal contradictions found. Where it loses ground: there is no functional-requirements table, no MoSCoW priority markers, and no UX section with empty/loading/error states at all, so unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements scores at the floor - a real gap given the brief explicitly asked for enough detail that engineering could size the work without a follow-up conversation. No stated measurement window for the primary metric. Open-questions ownership is honestly hedged (names 'regional ops managers' as a candidate but flags it as unconfirmed) rather than firmly assigned. Includes the long-haul-trucking distractor as a non-goal, which is defensible as a scope boundary but not information a disciplined author needed to volunteer. All 5 probes answerable from the text alone, including the ownership one, on the strength of the tentative owner named.

Template shell with no domain content at all - the title itself is an unrendered {{title}} placeholder. Every section exists (Summary through Appendix, all the full-variant headings) but every sentence is interchangeable corporate filler: 'stakeholders have indicated,' 'appropriate tracking will be put in place,' 'as appropriate.' Zero named people, counts, dates, or facts from the scenario appear anywhere - no Renata, no 12%, no DriverGo, no union rule, no VP commitment. This is the anti-form trap made literal: it has a Success metrics section with Primary/Guardrail/Measurement-window labels and a Functional requirements table with a Priority column, satisfying the letter of two rubric criteria while containing no actual metric or requirement. I scored those low anyway since the labels carry no content. None of the five retrieval probes are answerable from this document - it does not mention the union rest-day rule, DriverGo, long-haul trucking, or any stop condition. The no_internal_contradiction held-out criterion technically 'passes' only because there is nothing concrete enough to contradict, which is a vacuous pass, not a quality signal, and I scored it accordingly low rather than rewarding the absence of content.

The most complete document against the rubric: goals are phrased as outcomes, non-goals include two substantive scope cuts beyond the long-haul boilerplate (real-time route optimization, deferring end-to-end automated swaps to a fast-follow, each with a stated reason), the primary metric and guardrail are both named with an explicit 4-week measurement window, the functional-requirements table carries a MoSCoW priority on every row, and the UX section names explicit empty and error states (though not a loading state, which keeps it off a 5). The single open-questions row has a real owner and a phase-based needed-by. Held-out criteria: it names an explicit stop condition tied to the primary metric at mid-peak, and I found no outright contradiction, though FR-4 marks DriverGo auto-push as a Must while the rollout plan ships Phase 1 with that push still manual - a tension a strict reader could flag, resolved only by inferring the Musts apply once a hub reaches full rollout. Decision-vs-input traceability is the weakest held-out score: most scope calls (the two genuine non-goals, the fast-follow deferral) are stated as flat assertions with no signal of whether they were the author's own judgment or given direction, aside from the build-vs-buy line which does trace back to the prior vendor failure. Repeats the long-haul distractor twice (once in Non-goals, again in Target users), which is more redundant than Artifact A's single mention. All five probes answerable directly and unambiguously, including a clean, non-hedged owner for the rest-day rule enforcement.

Content-free. Every section is filled with placeholder abstraction: the Problem names no user, no frequency, no cost ('Stakeholders have indicated that certain aspects of the current experience could be improved'). The Problem section is no longer or more developed than the Solution overview, and neither says anything. Goals restate the problem ('Deliver an improved experience'); the Non-goals line excludes nothing by name. Target users is 'the relevant user groups'. Success metrics name no metric at all - 'Relevant indicators will be tracked' fails the primary/guardrail/window check three times over. Open questions is filled but with 'Team' and 'As appropriate', which is the placeholder the criterion explicitly rules out. UX names no empty, loading, or error state; the single FR carries a MoSCoW marker but describes 'the core capability needed', which nothing can be sized from. Held-out: nothing is scopable, no stop condition exists, and no decision is distinguishable from an input. It scores 2 rather than 1 on internal contradiction only vacuously - it makes no claim that could conflict with another. Zero of five probes answerable: the document does not mention long-haul, DriverGo, HR data, the rest-day rule, peak season, or any metric. It has the shape of a full PRD and none of the content.

Specific throughout and decision-useful. Problem carries real evidence with who/how often/cost - Renata Okafor's 3-4 hour Sunday rebuild, two double-bookings in a month, 12% of shifts reassigned on delivery day, swaps that never reach the sheet - and runs longer and more developed than the Solution overview. Metrics are the strongest section: primary (delays halved vs pre-peak baseline), a separately named guardrail (day-of reassignment at or below the 12% baseline), and a real window (4 weeks into peak vs 4 weeks prior), written pre-hoc. Open questions row has a named owner (regional ops managers) and a milestone (before Phase 1). Marked down where it is literally short: two of four goals are shipped features rather than outcomes; UX names empty, error, and an edge case but no loading state, so the unhappy-paths criterion is only partly met (3), even though every FR row does carry a MoSCoW priority. Held-out: dependency rows carry owner and status and the NFRs carry measurable targets, so most of it is scopable, though FR-1 ('build a proposed weekly schedule from availability') is the one load-bearing row too broad to size. Stop condition exists but is buried in a risk-table mitigation cell ('stop and reassess if the primary metric shows no gain at mid-peak'). No contradictions found - FR-5 (record a swap) and the non-goal (no automated end-to-end swaps) are consistent. Weakest held-out is decided-vs-told (3): it flags a few ('Marcus Feld has committed publicly', 'this is a build, not a buy', shift swaps 'a likely fast follow') but most of the document reports in a flat voice. Distractors: the Finance $50k budget board is absent; long-haul appears only as a one-line non-goal, which the scope question requires. All five probes answerable.

Strong on decision-usefulness, materially incomplete as a deliverable. Best-in-set on three held-out checks: a dedicated Stop condition tied to concrete triggers (no demonstrable delay reduction by peak, or inability to enforce the 6-day rule); an explicit 'What we're told vs. what we're concluding' section that makes authorship traceable; and no contradiction I can name, though Next steps commits engineering sizing while the Risks section says build-vs-buy should be confirmed before committing engineering time - a tension, not a conflict. It is also honest where honesty costs it: it states the 'schedule-related' delay baseline does not exist and calls establishing it a prerequisite workstream. Problem is evidence-dense and analytically sharp (two distinct failure modes), scored 4 rather than 5 for the unsourced 'scales linearly with hub count, not driver count per hub' claim. Where it loses: no Functional requirements at all, so no MoSCoW priorities, and no UX section, so no empty, loading, or error states - a 1 on that criterion. Metrics give a primary and a deadline but no separately framed guardrail and no measurement window (3). Target users is a single line naming schedulers and ops managers with no situational detail (3). The open question about rule-violation sign-off proposes regional ops managers before design locks, but is prose rather than an owned, dated row (3). Held-out scopability suffers for the same reason (2): there are no requirement, NFR, or dependency rows to size, and no flows to sketch, which is precisely what the brief asked for. Distractors: Finance absent; long-haul handled at slightly more length than the exclusion warrants. All five probes answerable, including the ownership probe (regional ops managers, flagged as needing confirmation).

Strongest problem section: names the scheduler, the 3-4 hr rebuild, the twice-repeated double-booking error, and the 12% reassignment rate, and it visibly outweighs the terser Solution overview. Primary metric, guardrail, and an explicit 8-week pre/post measurement window are all stated before any result exists. Explicit, concrete stop condition tied to the peak-season date. FR table carries Must/Should on every row; UX section names an empty state and an error state (though not loading), which is real unhappy-path content, not just a heading. Held down from a higher rubric mean because two of the three Open questions/Dependencies rows and one Goal exist only to carry the $50k budget-review distractor, and one Goal and one Non-goal are feature-shaped rather than outcome-shaped - a senior reviewer would cut that row, so it can't score a 5 there. Decision-vs-input traceability is present only structurally (Context attributes claims to named people) but the doc never marks 'we decided' vs 'we were told' inline. Includes both scenario distractors (the $50k finance threshold and the long-haul division), which is a discipline gap, not a completeness gain.

Best-in-panel on two axes: an explicit 'What we're told vs. what we're concluding' section that is exactly the decision-vs-input traceability the held-out criterion looks for, and the clearest risk ranking of the three ('single highest-risk dependency... close second'). Honest and non-circular about metrics - it flags that no schedule-related-delay baseline exists yet rather than inventing one, which is more mature than asserting a window it can't back, but it means the literal 'measurement window' the rubric checks for is not present. That same rigor exposes the real gap: no functional-requirements list, no priority markers, no NFR table, no dependency table, no rollout plan, and no empty/loading/error-state coverage in any form. The scenario's ask was explicit that engineering must be able to size the work and design must be able to start sketching without a follow-up conversation - B is a strong strategic brief but does not clear that bar on its own text, so the gap is substance, not form. Includes the long-haul distractor, elaborated across three sentences, more attention than any other artifact gives it; does not include the $50k-budget distractor.

Generic boilerplate: the title placeholder ({{title}}) is unfilled, and no fact from the scenario (Denver, Renata, DriverGo, the 6-consecutive-day rule, the VP's 50% target, the 340 drivers, the prior SaaS cancellation) appears anywhere in the document. Every section restates its own heading in vaguer words ('relevant indicators will be tracked', 'an appropriate period following rollout'). Target user is explicitly the undifferentiated 'relevant user groups' the rubric criterion names as the failure case. Open questions row has no real owner ('Team') and no real date ('As appropriate'). Scored the internal-contradiction criterion a 1 rather than crediting it for vacuous consistency: there is nothing concrete enough in the document to cross-check, and treating that absence as a pass would reward having no content. None of the five probes are answerable from this document alone.

Problem section is strong and clearly outweighs the thin solution description: named individual (3-4 hrs, repeated double-booking), a quarter-level stat (12% manual reassignment), and a second, distinct failure mode (informal swap drift). Explicitly separates 'what we're told' from 'what we're concluding,' which is exactly the kind of decision-vs-input traceability a reader can point to. Has a real, dated-to-an-event stop condition tied to two concrete triggers (delay reduction, rest-day enforcement), and no internal contradictions found. Where it falls short of the ask: there is no functional-requirements table, no NFR targets, no UX/unhappy-path detail, and no structured open-questions table with owner+date rows -- the closest is a paragraph naming 'regional ops managers' as a tentative owner pending confirmation, which is enough to answer the probe but not enough for engineering to size work without a follow-up conversation, which the brief asked for explicitly. Non-goals reduces to a single scope exclusion, and that exclusion is one of the scenario's flagged distractor facts (the long-haul division) rather than a considered trade-off. Goals and success metrics are present but merged into one section without a stated measurement window.

An unfilled template shell: literal placeholder text in the title, and every section is generic boilerplate with no scenario-specific facts, names, numbers, or dates anywhere in the document (no driver counts, no named stakeholders, no metric values, no dependencies). Nothing here lets a reader answer any of the five probes -- there is no problem evidence, no named user segment, no metric, no dependency, and no rule owner because none of these are ever instantiated with real content. Table structures exist (FR, NFR, dependencies, risks, open questions) but every cell is filled with vague filler ('the system will support the core capability needed'), so the tables provide no more scoping value than empty ones. No internal claim is specific enough to contradict another, which is a vacuous pass on that one check, not a sign of quality.

The most operationally complete of the three: FR rows are concrete and individually sizable (e.g. a specific consecutive-day block rule, a specific cross-check requirement), NFRs carry numeric targets, dependencies carry an owner and a status column, and a bolded stop condition is tied to a specific date-before-peak trigger. Success metrics name a primary, a guardrail, and an explicit pre/post measurement window. Two genuine non-goals (no swap auto-approval, no DriverGo UI redesign) sit alongside a third that restates one of the scenario's flagged distractor facts (the long-haul exclusion), and that same distractor plus the Finance budget-review distractor each appear twice more, in Target users, Dependencies, and Open questions -- four distractor mentions total, the most of the three documents, which is undisciplined padding rather than added completeness. Decision-vs-input separation is present but lighter than a dedicated section: an appendix lists source facts and a few inline '(VP commitment)'-style tags, rather than prose that consistently marks which calls were the author's own versus handed down.

Content-free. Every section is a filled-in shape with no scenario facts in it: no drivers, no hubs, no DriverGo, no union rule, no VP, no numbers, no names. It has a Success metrics heading with three bullets and states no metric ('relevant indicators will be tracked'), which is precisely the failure the anti-form warning points at, inverted - this is form with nothing underneath. Problem section (1) cites no evidence and is no more developed than the Solution overview; goals (1) are 'deliver an improved experience' with a non-goal that excludes nothing; target user (1) is 'the relevant user groups'; metrics (1) name none; open questions (1) list owner 'Team' / needed-by 'As appropriate', a placeholder dressed as a filled row; UX (1) gestures at 'typical and atypical scenarios' with no empty/loading/error state, though the FR table does carry one MoSCoW value on its single row. Held-out: unscopable (1) - not one row is sizable; no stop condition (1); decided-vs-told (1) is a flat undifferentiated voice throughout. It scores 3 on no_internal_contradiction only vacuously - nothing contradicts because nothing is asserted - and I credited that literally rather than punishing it twice. Zero probes answerable. It also cannot include distractors, which is not discipline, just emptiness.

Substantively complete and specific, and its advantage over C is content, not shape. Problem (4): Renata, 3-4h Sunday rebuild, same double-booking twice in a month, 12% day-of reassignment, and it explicitly grades its own evidence ('one region's data point, but corroborated by a harder number'); Problem runs longer than Solution overview. Goals/non-goals (4): 'cut schedule-related delivery delays in half before peak' is an outcome, three non-goals each carry a reason - though 'enforce the union rule automatically' is a feature sitting in a goals list. Target user (4): regional scheduler, one per hub, 9 total. Metrics (4): primary 50% delay reduction, separate guardrail (zero rest-day violations), explicit 8-week pre/post window - the only artifact with all three; it does assume a schedule-related-delay baseline exists, which C correctly says does not. Open questions (4): three rows, real team owners, real milestones. Weakest rubric line is unhappy paths (3): UX names an empty state and an error state but no loading state, though MoSCoW is on every FR row. Held-out: stop condition (5) is the sharpest in the set - a dated checkpoint six weeks pre-peak, a threshold, an action, and a fallback (run peak on the spreadsheet); scopable (4) - measurable NFR targets (5 min, 99%), owned dependency rows with status; decided-vs-told (4) is real but scattered ('(VP commitment)', 'that deadline, not general appetite for tooling, is why'); no-contradiction (4) - no nameable conflicting pair, but the 8-week post-launch window sits awkwardly against a staged 9-hub rollout running up to peak. All 5 probes answerable. Penalised for distractors: the $50k Finance review board appears twice, as a dependency row and an open question - roughly a quarter of those two tables spent on procurement trivia that belongs nowhere near this PRD. That lapse is why this is a 4 and not higher.

The best thinking in the set and the least complete deliverable. Problem (5) is the strongest single section anywhere here: same evidence as B, plus the observation that slow construction and post-construction drift are two distinct failure modes and fixing one will not fix the other. Decided-vs-told (5) is not incidental - there is a 'What we're told vs. what we're concluding' section, and the SaaS history is read correctly ('evidence a generic tool won't fit, not evidence that building is automatically the right call'). It is also the more disciplined artifact on distractors: no $50k budget board anywhere, and long-haul appears only as an explicit exclusion with a reason, which probe 1 demands. Where it loses is delivery, not layout - I checked that I was not marking it down for lacking headings. Metrics (3): primary and guardrail present and honestly framed (it flags that no schedule-related-delay baseline exists and calls establishing it a prerequisite - a better call than B's assumed baseline), but no measurement window, only a deadline. Unhappy paths and prioritised requirements (1): no functional requirements at all, so nothing to prioritise, and no empty/loading/error states - 'sketch the rebuild flow and the override view' is not a state description. That cascades into scopable_without_a_meeting (2): there is no FR, NFR target, or dependency row to size; it names the blockers well (DriverGo, HR feed, spikes needed) but hands engineering nothing to estimate, against an ask that explicitly required engineering be able to size it without coming back. Open questions (4) live in prose but carry an owner (regional ops managers, with HR/compliance) and a milestone ('before design locks the escalation path'). Stop condition (4) is present but triggers at peak-season start, arguably too late to act on, versus B's six-weeks-prior checkpoint. No-contradiction (4). All 5 probes answerable.

Problem section is evidenced and outweighs Solution overview in length and specificity (Renata Okafor named, 3-4hr rebuild, double-booked twice, 12% day-of reassignment rate), and honestly hedges that the 12% figure is Denver-sourced rather than company-wide, flagging the extrapolation as an open question rather than asserting it. Goals are outcome-framed (delay cut, build-time cut, structural rest-rule enforcement) and all three non-goals carry a stated reason. Target users are specific (named scheduler role, 340 drivers/9 hubs, explicit 'not built for long-haul dispatchers'). Success metrics give a named primary, a named guardrail, and a stated 4-week pre/post measurement window. Open questions have named owners (regional ops, DriverGo eng) and milestone-based due points, not TBD. FR table carries full MoSCoW priority. UX section covers empty, error, and edge-case explicitly but never names a loading state, the one clean rubric gap. Held-out: names an explicit, dated stop/escalate condition tied to a named executive; FR/NFR/Dependencies tables are specific enough to size, though DriverGo and HR-feed rows are honestly marked 'unconfirmed' rather than falsely precise; one minor tension between the Dependencies row assigning rest-rule sign-off to regional ops and an Open Question re-asking who should own it, which keeps no_internal_contradiction off a perfect score. Handles both scenario distractors correctly: omits the finance/budget-review fact entirely and states the long-haul exclusion in one disciplined non-goal line rather than dwelling on it. All 5 retrieval probes answerable directly from the document.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this artifact opens with a first-person note stating the writer's Read call surfaced the scenario's hidden Retrieval-probes and Distractors sections before drafting, and asks the harness to discard or flag the run. That is not something a real PRD deliverable would ever contain, and it means this document's unusually tight alignment to the exact probe questions and its clean avoidance of both distractors cannot be taken as demonstrated authoring skill under blind conditions -- I am reporting what is on the page but discounting the apparent probe/distractor performance accordingly and flagging it as a validity concern for the harness. On the substance: Problem section is evidenced (same Okafor/12%/DriverGo/HR facts as A) but states the 12% reassignment rate as company-wide without the source ambiguity A discloses -- a small overreach. Non-goals are present with reasons, but there is no separate Goals section; goals must be inferred from Success criteria, which works but is structurally thinner. Target users section names three specific personas. Success criteria give a primary, a guardrail, and a stated peak-window, though one metric ('a target we'll confirm... during design') is left undefined. Open-questions handling is the weak point: there is no Open Questions table at all -- ownership is asserted once in prose ('Regional ops managers own validation... before any hub goes live') without the structured owner+date rows the criterion looks for. There is no UX/design section and no functional-requirements table with per-row priority at all -- for a document meant to let engineering size and design start sketching, this is a real gap, not a nitpick. Held-out: the 'Stop / reconsider condition' section is excellent and explicit; but without FR/NFR/Dependency tables the document is harder to size line-by-line without a conversation; the decision-vs-input distinction is genuinely well handled (an explicit author-confidence calibration up front, and 'that's evidence for X, but...' framing elsewhere). All 5 retrieval probes are answerable from the document, but see caveat above about what that indicates.

Unfilled template: the title itself is still the literal placeholder '{{title}}'. Every section is generic boilerplate with no scenario facts at all -- no Denver, no Okafor, no DriverGo, no union rest-rule, no VP mandate, no hub/driver counts. Goals, non-goals, target users, metrics, dependencies, and open questions are all vague placeholder prose ('a relevant indicator of user value will be tracked', 'to be determined', 'certain aspects... remain to be finalized'), which is exactly the not-TBD failure mode the rubric calls out by name. The single FR row is untestable filler. No stop condition, no scoping detail an engineer could size, no traceable decisions. The only reason no_internal_contradiction scores above 1 is that there is no actual content to contradict -- a vacuous pass, not a demonstrated quality, so it is scored low rather than rewarded. None of the 5 retrieval probes can be answered from this document.

Strong evidenced Problem section (Renata Okafor, 3-4hr rebuild, two double-bookings, 12% day-of reassignment rate, 340 drivers/9 hubs) that is longer and more developed than the short 'What we're building' list. Named, situated user segments (schedulers/drivers/ops managers). Explicit, well-formed stop/reconsider condition tied to the peak deadline, and unusually good decision-vs-input traceability (an explicit 'author confidence' note separating sourced facts from proposed, uncommitted solution shape). All 5 probes answerable directly from the text. But it has no Goals section as such (success criteria do double duty, functionally adequate but not labeled), no guardrail metric distinguished from the primary, and critically no Open Questions table (no owned/dated open items) and no prioritized/MoSCoW requirements or UX empty/loading/error-state coverage at all -- a real gap against the ask's explicit requirement that design could start sketching and engineering could size work without follow-up. Handles the long-haul-trucking fact correctly (one-line non-goal, not dwelt on) and omits the finance/budget-review distractor entirely. Process note at the top (flagging that the scenario's probes/distractors were inadvertently visible before drafting) is a disclosure about production, not part of the document's content, and was not used to adjust scoring -- I scored the PRD text on its own merits.

Unfilled template: literal '{{title}}' placeholder, and every section is generic boilerplate with no facts from the brief at all -- no Renata, no 12%, no DriverGo, no union rest-day rule, no VP mandate, no hub/driver counts. Owners are 'To be determined', the single FR is untestable ('the core capability described in the solution overview'), success metrics name no real indicator or window, and there is no stop condition. None of the 5 retrieval probes can be answered from this document -- it does not even mention drivers, scheduling, or the union rule, so it is not merely weak on this scenario, it reads as a generic skeleton not written for it. No internal contradictions were found, but only because nothing concrete is asserted to contradict. No distractor facts appear, but that is not a virtue here since nothing else does either.

Hits every rubric criterion concretely: Problem section is evidenced (Renata Okafor, 12%, informal texting) and explicitly caveats that Denver's severity is not yet confirmed company-wide; Goals are outcome-phrased (delay reduction, build-time target, rest-rule made structurally impossible) with three Non-goals each carrying a stated reason; target users are named and situated; Success metrics explicitly label Primary, Guardrail, and Measurement window; Open Questions has three rows with real owners (regional ops managers, DriverGo eng team) and real milestones; Functional requirements carry MoSCoW priority (Must/Should/Won't) and UX and design names explicit empty, error, and edge-case states. Held-out criteria are also strong: an explicit stop-and-reassess checkpoint tied to a named escalation path, no internal contradictions found across goals/non-goals/FRs/rollout, and clear separation of stated leadership mandate from the author's own added goals and scope calls. All 5 probes answerable, including the riskiest-dependency probe (DriverGo write-API risk called out twice, in both Risks and Dependencies). Handles both distractors correctly: long-haul trucking gets one non-goal line, and the finance/budget-review fact does not appear. Not given a 5: several load-bearing rows (DriverGo integration, HR data feed) are marked 'Unconfirmed - not yet scoped,' so engineering still needs a spike before firm sizing on the two riskiest items, and the document proposes several company-wide goals/FRs before the open question of whether Denver's severity generalizes to the other 8 hubs is resolved -- mitigated by the phased Denver-first rollout, but still a live gap a senior reviewer would flag.

Content-free boilerplate. Nothing in it is specific to any situation: no counts, no quotes, no named people, no systems, no numbers. Problem section asserts 'stakeholders have identified a number of challenges' with zero evidence (1). The single Goal is 'deliver a solution that meaningfully improves the experience' - a shipped-thing restatement, and the Non-goal is an explicit placeholder ('efforts that fall outside the current scope will be considered separately') (1). Target users are 'individuals and teams who regularly encounter the situation described above' - undifferentiated (1). Success metrics name no metric at all: 'a relevant indicator of user value will be tracked', 'an appropriate period' - no primary, no guardrail, no window (1). Open questions row reads 'Certain aspects of the approach remain to be finalized / To be determined / Prior to launch' - the exact TBD placeholder the criterion forbids (1). UX section names no empty, loading, or error state; the FR table has a single row carrying a 'Should' marker but the row itself ('the system will support the core capability described in the solution overview') is unsizeable (1). Held-out: nothing is scopable - every dependency owner is 'To be determined' (1); no stop or kill condition anywhere (1); no_internal_contradiction passes only VACUOUSLY - the document asserts nothing concrete enough to conflict with anything else, so I score 3 rather than crediting it as a real cross-check (3); voice is flat and undifferentiated throughout, no way to tell an author's call from a directive (1). It also omits the finance distractor only vacuously - it omits everything - so that is not to its credit. All five probes unanswerable. This is the anti-form case: complete headings, correct section order, confident register, zero content.

Strongest of the three. Problem carries the specific evidence (Renata Okafor's 3-4 hour Sunday rebuild, two double-bookings in a month, 12% day-of reassignment last quarter) and explicitly bounds its own generalization: 'We have this evidence for Denver specifically; we do not yet have equivalent data from the other 8 hubs.' Scored 4 not 5 on problem_weight because the Problem section only modestly outweighs the Solution overview in development, and the tie-break is downward. Goals are outcomes (halve delays, 3-4 hours to under 30 minutes) and each Non-goal states a reason (5). Target user is the regional scheduler, one per hub, with the situation named; secondary 340 drivers (4). Metrics has a named primary, a real guardrail (zero rest-rule violations) and a window - but the section contradicts itself: primary says 'measured before the November-December peak' while the window says 'the 4 weeks into peak season'. That defect caps metrics at 4 and is the reason no_internal_contradiction scores 3; I can name both sentences and they are in the same section. Open questions carry team owners and needed-by milestones (5). UX gives empty, error and edge states but no loading state, so 4 despite full MoSCoW priorities including a Won't row. Held-out: dependencies carry owners and honest status ('Unconfirmed - not yet scoped'), NFRs carry measurable targets (5-minute sync, 9 hubs / 340 drivers), so an engineer could size most of it (4). Stop condition present but framed as escalate-before-full-rollout rather than halt (4). Decision-vs-input is the best in the set: 'leadership's stated bar', 'That deadline, not general modernization, is why this is being proposed now' (5). Probes: 5/5. Probe 5 reading stated explicitly - I counted the dependency row 'Regional ops sign-off on rest-rule logic | Regional ops managers' as naming a real owner; the open question about who FORMALLY owns validation refines rather than erases that, but a stricter reading would score this 4/5. Distractors: correctly omits the finance $50k budget-board rule; the long-haul mention is a one-line non-goal, which the non-goals criterion and probe 1 both require, so not penalized.

Substantively strong prose, structurally incomplete against what the ask required. Opens with meta-process text addressed to a harness rather than to leadership - verbatim: 'Note on process: the Read tool returned the entire scenario file in one call, including the "Retrieval probes" and "Distractors" sections I was instructed not to read... Flagging this so the harness can discard or flag draft 2 accordingly.' I report that as document content; a leadership-facing PRD carrying it is defective as a deliverable, and it costs C holistically. I did not discount its probe count on that basis. Problem is the best-written in the set - evidenced, and it outweighs 'What we're building' (5). Goals appear only as Success criteria, with reasoned Out of scope entries (4). Target users are three named roles with their situations (4). Metrics: primary and window present, and 'zero union rest-rule violations reaching an active schedule' functions as a guardrail, but one criterion is openly deferred - 'a target we'll confirm with schedulers during design' (4). No Open questions section at all: unknowns appear as prose with no owners and no dates, and only the Ownership section names anyone against a milestone (2). No UX or design section, therefore no empty, loading or error states, and the five build items are an unprioritized numbered list with no MoSCoW - the ask specifically wanted design able to sketch and engineering able to size without coming back, and both would come back (1). Held-out: not scopable - no dependency owners, no statuses, no measurable NFR targets, one success target explicitly postponed (2). But it has the cleanest stop condition of the three, a dedicated 'Stop / reconsider condition' section tied to trend, runway and rule reliability (5). no_internal_contradiction 4: the softest tension is 'Regional ops managers, who need visibility into swap activity and rule compliance' against 'Historical schedule analytics and reporting dashboards are deferred to a later phase' - I judged these can coexist (live visibility is not historical reporting), so it stays 4 on that reading rather than on splitting the difference. decision_vs_input is excellent, including an explicit confidence split: 'High on the operational facts... lower on solution shape, which is a proposed starting point, not a committed design' (5). Probes 5/5. Distractors: finance $50k rule correctly omitted; long-haul is a scoped exclusion, not padding.

Problem section names a specific scheduler, a quantified rebuild time, a repeat error, and a 12% reassignment rate, and is longer/denser than the one-paragraph solution overview. Goals are outcomes (delay cut, build-time cut, rest-rule structurally enforced) and all three non-goals carry a stated reason. Target users split primary/secondary with the situation named. Success metrics give a named primary, a named guardrail, and an explicit pre/post measurement window. Open questions carry role-based owners and milestone dates, not TBD. UX section has explicit empty/error/edge-case text and every FR row carries a MoSCoW priority. Held-out: a real stop trigger exists (escalate to the VP if the 6-week pre-peak checkpoint isn't trending down), no contradiction found between goals/non-goals/rollout, and the document distinguishes the VP's mandate from the author's own inference in a couple of places. Avoids both distractors (no Finance/$50k mention; long-haul trucking appears only as a one-line non-goal, matching what the probe requires rather than dwelling on it). One real flaw: it labels the 12%-reassignment stat as 'Denver-specific evidence' and manufactures an open question about whether other hubs match it, but the source fact as given wasn't scoped to Denver in the first place - a minor invented-uncertainty issue, not a fabrication. All five probes answerable. Strong, but the Denver-scoping slip and the build-time goal not carrying through into a tracked success metric are the kind of nitpick that keeps this at 'solid, shippable' rather than untouchable.

Problem framing is the most developed of the three - it ties the spreadsheet, the DriverGo disconnect, informal text swaps, and unchecked certifications into one coherent failure picture, clearly outweighing the solution section. Out-of-scope items each carry a reason. Target users are named and specific (three named roles, not 'all users'). Primary metric and guardrail are present, though the build-time target is explicitly left undetermined ('a target we'll confirm... during design'), which weakens 'defined before build.' The dedicated 'Stop / reconsider condition' section is excellent - clearer and more explicit than Artifact A's version - and the top-line confidence statement plus the 'why now' reasoning cleanly separate the VP's stated mandate from the author's own inference, satisfying the decision-traceability check well. But two rubric items fail outright: there is no Open Questions table at all (the closest analogue, an 'Ownership' line, names an owner but not a dated question), and there is no UX/design section with empty/loading/error states and no MoSCoW priority on any requirement - both of which the scenario's own ask explicitly calls for ('so engineering can size it and design can start sketching'). The DriverGo risk is honestly flagged as needing a spike before it can be sized, which is candid but means that row fails 'scopable without a meeting' by the rubric's own definition. The document also opens with a stray process note about the drafting conditions that does not belong in a PRD meant for leadership review - a senior reader would immediately flag it as out of place. All five probes still answerable from the substantive content. Strong on judgment and honesty, but missing structured deliverables the ask required.

Fully generic mail-merge document - the title placeholder itself is unfilled ('{{title}}'), and every section is templated boilerplate with no specific facts, numbers, names, or decisions ('stakeholders have identified a number of challenges,' 'an appropriate period following release'). No named problem or evidence, no measurable goal, no named user segment, no named metric or window, an empty-in-substance open question with owner 'To be determined,' and no unhappy-path UX description. The one FR row technically carries a priority marker ('Should') but the requirement text is a placeholder pointing back at the solution overview, not an actual requirement, so it doesn't functionally satisfy the criterion. No stop condition, no traceable decisions, and trivially no internal contradiction only because there is nothing concrete enough to contradict. None of the five retrieval probes can be answered from this document - it contains no scenario-specific facts at all.

Strong, well-evidenced Problem section (named scheduler, hours, error count, quarterly rate) that clearly outweighs the short Solution list. Explicit, well-labeled ownership statement and a genuinely hard stop/reconsider condition tied to metrics and the peak deadline - the strongest stop condition of the three. Author explicitly separates evidenced fact from proposed judgment ('Author confidence' line, 'Why now' reasoning vs. the VP's stated mandate), which is rare and valuable. But it is missing structural content the ask itself calls for, not just formatting: no UX/design section at all (so design has nothing to sketch from, contrary to the brief), no priority markers on the five 'what we're building' items (engineering can't tell what's cut first), and no owned/dated open-questions table (ownership and unknowns are named in prose but not tied to dates, except one milestone). Includes the long-haul-trucking exclusion as a non-goal, which the scenario flags as a distractor, though it is used in a defensible, reasoned way rather than as filler. All five probes answerable.

Template placeholder document - the title field itself is an unresolved '{{title}}' token. Every section is generic filler with no scenario-specific fact: no named user, no number, no dollar figure, no metric, no date. The FR table technically carries a 'Priority' column and the UX section technically gestures at 'typical and edge cases,' but neither names anything checkable, which is exactly the form-over-substance failure the anti-form instruction warns against - the shape of a PRD with none of the content. No distractors appear only because no real facts of any kind appear. Zero of the five probes are answerable from this document.

The most complete document: Problem section carries the same named evidence as A plus an explicit admission that the evidence is Denver-specific and routed to an owned, dated open question - a self-aware move the other two lack. Goals are outcomes, non-goals are reasoned (though one is the long-haul-trucking distractor), success metrics are explicitly labeled Primary/Guardrail/Window, every FR carries a MoSCoW tag, and the open-questions table has a named owner and a needed-by milestone on every row - the two criteria Artifact A leaves weakest are exactly the two this document nails. An appendix explicitly traces each claim to its source, which is a strong instance of decision-vs-input traceability. Held back from a 5 by real nitpicks a senior reviewer would flag: the UX section covers empty, error, and edge states but not loading; the closest thing to a stop/kill condition is a 6-week checkpoint that 'escalates' to the VP rather than stating the initiative would actually stop or be cut back; and an NFR ('Reliability: DriverGo reflects the record within 5 minutes') is really a latency target mislabeled. All five probes answerable, one (the stop condition) only marginally so given the escalate-not-stop phrasing.

Content-free. Every section is a grammatically correct placeholder that names nothing: no scheduler, no hub count, no 12% reassignment rate, no 3-4 hour rebuild, no DriverGo, no union rest rule, no peak-season deadline. Problem section is three sentences of abstraction and is no more developed than the Solution overview. Goals restate 'improve the experience'; the single non-goal excludes nothing. Target users are 'individuals and teams who regularly encounter the situation described above' - an undifferentiated everyone. Success metrics name a metric only by category: 'A relevant indicator of user value will be tracked' with 'an appropriate period' as the window - this is the anti-form test's canonical failure, a well-ordered document with the metric missing. Open questions row is 'Certain aspects of the approach remain to be finalized' / 'To be determined' / 'Prior to launch': a filled table used as decoration. FR-1 carries a MoSCoW 'Should' but describes nothing testable, and UX names no empty, loading, or error state. Held-out: nothing is scopable (every dependency owner is TBD, every NFR target is 'acceptable'); no stop condition at any threshold; no contradiction only because it asserts nothing falsifiable, which is not a pass on decision-usefulness; and the flat voice makes every statement indistinguishable between authored judgment and received instruction. All five probes unanswerable. Its 1s come from emptiness, not from distractor inclusion - it includes no facts at all, including none of the distractors.

Substantively the strongest. Problem carries named, quantified evidence (Renata Okafor, 3-4 hours, two double-bookings in a month, 12% day-of reassignment, untracked text swaps) and out-weighs the Solution overview. Metrics are the cleanest of the three: labelled primary (50% delay cut), a genuinely separate guardrail (zero rest-rule violations in published schedules), and a stated window (4 weeks pre-launch baseline vs first 4 weeks of peak). Every FR carries a MoSCoW mark including an explicit Won't (FR-6) that matches its own non-goal - no internal contradiction found on a Goals/Non-goals/FR/NFR/rollout cross-check. Dependencies carry owners and honest 'Unconfirmed' statuses; open questions carry team owners and milestone gates. Decision-vs-input is the best in the set: 'leadership's stated bar', 'That deadline, not general modernization, is why this is proposed now', an explicit v1 scope call on swap approval, and an appendix listing source facts. Defects, all real: (1) it recasts the company-wide 12% reassignment rate as 'Denver-specific evidence' and then builds an open question ('Is Denver's 12% typical of other hubs?') on that misreading - a factual distortion of the brief, and why problem evidence is 4 not 5; (2) UX names empty, error, and an edge case but no loading state, so unhappy-path coverage is incomplete - 3; (3) FR-1 ('generate a draft weekly schedule from availability') is load-bearing and too vague to size, which is what holds scopable_without_a_meeting to 3; (4) stop condition is an escalation, not a halt - 'checkpoint 6 weeks pre-peak; escalate to Marcus Feld' plus a Denver rollback, so held-out stop/kill is 3 even though probe 2 is answerable. That 5/5-probe alongside a 3 on stop/kill is deliberate, not an arithmetic slip: the probe asks whether a reader can answer the question, the criterion asks whether the document commits to halting. Does not include the finance/$50k budget-board distractor.

Best prose and the best answer to two held-out criteria; materially incomplete against the ask. Strengths: a dedicated 'Stop / reconsider condition' section tying a concrete trigger (delay/reassignment rates not trending toward the peak target with runway before November, or unreliable rest-rule enforcement) to a stated action, which nothing else in the set does - the only weakness there is undefined 'enough runway'. An 'Author confidence' header separates sourced operational facts from proposed solution shape, and the buy-vs-build reasoning is visibly the author's own inference from the cancelled-vendor fact. Problem section is evidenced and clearly out-weighs 'What we're building'. Where it fails is substance the rubric asks for, not formatting: no Open questions table at all - the unknowns name spikes and audits but no owner and no date, so open_questions_owned_and_dated is 2, with the Ownership section rescuing only the rest-rule item; no UX section, therefore no empty, loading, or error states, and no MoSCoW priority on any of the five numbered requirements, so unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements is 1. There are no NFR targets, no dependency rows with owner/status, and no rollout or release plan, which collectively make scopable_without_a_meeting a 2 - engineering cannot size and, given the scenario's explicit ask, design cannot start sketching from this. Success criteria are outcomes but unlabelled as primary/guardrail, and one is openly deferred ('a target we'll confirm with schedulers'). Separately, the artifact opens with an eval-harness process note ('the Read tool returned the entire scenario file... including the Retrieval probes and Distractors sections') sitting above a document marked 'Draft for leadership review'. Judged as delivered, that is non-document text at the top of a stakeholder deliverable and it counts against the artifact. Does not include the finance/$50k distractor.

Rubric (4,4,4,3,4,2 -> 3.5): Problem section is concretely evidenced (22-min baseline, 40% error rate, $18/resubmission, n=214 survey, 35% 65+ segment) and is longer than the Solution overview section. Goals mix outcomes (reduce time, reduce error rate) with one milestone (Oct 1 go-live); non-goals each carry a stated reason (budget for kiosks, unscoped for voice-to-text, no data for no-show). Target users names a primary segment (new-patient intake, including the 65+ cohort and its specific friction) and a secondary (front desk staff, Riverside's FTE gap) rather than 'all users.' Metrics are present but scattered across Goals and the Rollout success gate rather than consolidated into one metrics section with a clearly separated primary vs. guardrail. Open questions table has two rows, each with a named owner (IT director + practice administrator; practice administration) and a milestone-based needed-by. Weakest: no UX/design section and no empty/loading/error-state coverage at all; the FR table does carry per-row MoSCoW priority (Must/Should/Won't), which is the one piece of criterion 6 it satisfies. Held-out (3,5,4,4 -> 4.0): FR/NFR/Dependency rows carry priority, target, owner, and status, but lack effort sizing, so an engineer could size some but not all rows without asking a question. Explicit stop condition is stated twice (Risks table and Rollout: expansion pauses if intake time or complaints exceed baseline in month one). On no-contradiction: FR-5 states the EHR integration target flatly as '(Epic)' and marks it Must, while the Open Questions table simultaneously lists 'Is the EHR Epic or athenahealth?' as unresolved and needed before integration begins -- a real tension between an already-committed requirement and a still-open question, even though the Dependencies row explains the intent (build toward Epic, but block on confirmation). Decision-vs-input is fairly traceable: the June 'no rush' email is named and explicitly superseded, the kiosk exclusion is tied to the budget figure, and rollout sequencing authority is attributed by name to Carla Nguyen rather than reported in a flat, undifferentiated voice. Probes: all 5 answerable directly from the text (Oct 1 target and Q1 supersession; pilot pause trigger; $16k gap and patient-owned-device resolution; Carla Nguyen's sign-off authority; Epic-per-IT with the athenahealth conflict flagged). Distractor discipline: mentions 2 of 3 (voice-to-text and no-show speculation, each framed as a reasoned non-goal); omits the GDPR aside entirely.

Rubric (5,4,3,5,2,1 -> 3.33): Problem section is the stronger of the two on this criterion -- names the front-desk-manager source, quantifies cost and error rate, and explicitly names the tension between the 72% device-preference survey stat and the 65+ tablet-struggle stat ('Both are true; the design has to serve both'). Goal statement is phrased as an outcome, and non-goals are reasoned (kiosk hardware to the Budget section, voice-to-text to timeline risk, no-show claim to absent data). No dedicated Target users section exists; the primary and secondary segments and their situations are inferable from the Problem section but never named as a discrete segment description, weaker than a structured callout. Metrics section is the strongest of the two: explicit primary measures (intake time, complaint volume, error rate under 10% but honestly flagged as unverified) plus a distinctly labeled 'Rollback trigger (leadership-set)' guardrail with a first-month window, written as pre-committed rather than fitted after the fact. Open questions is thin: one EHR issue is raised with an implied owner (practice administrator) and a milestone ('before integration work starts'), but there is no multi-row owned/dated table the way Artifact A has one. Weakest: no functional-requirements table at all, so there is no per-row MoSCoW marking and no empty/loading/error-state treatment -- prioritization exists only at the coarse in-scope/out-of-scope level. Held-out (2,5,5,5 -> 4.25): scoping without a meeting is harder here than in A because there are no ID'd, priority-tagged requirement rows to size individually, just narrative scope bullets. Stop/kill condition is the clearest of the two documents, explicitly labeled a 'hard gate, not a guideline.' No internal contradiction found across Scope, Budget, and Compliance. Decision-vs-input traceability is strong and explicit throughout: 'This document treats Epic as the integration target, per IT, since IT owns the technical relationship,' the Q1 email is called 'stale' rather than silently dropped, and the no-show claim is attributed to 'one team member' and explicitly rejected as unsupported rather than folded in flatly. Probes: all 5 answerable directly (Oct 1 target with the Q1 email marked stale; the labeled rollback trigger; the $16k gap resolved via patient-owned devices plus a smaller assisted-fallback tablet count; Carla Nguyen's sign-off under a dedicated 'Decision authority' heading; Epic-per-IT as the stated target with the conflict flagged as an open issue). Distractor discipline is the weakest point: all 3 distractors appear, including a dedicated Compliance bullet on GDPR that resolves a non-issue the scenario never asked resolved -- the clearest case of noise inclusion between the two documents.

Strong prose PRD with excellent decision-traceability (explicit 'Recommendation:' framing on the budget fix, explicit reasoning for choosing Epic over athenahealth, explicit treatment of the June-vs-October timeline conflict) and an explicit, hard-gate rollback trigger. No internal contradictions found. All 5 probes answerable from the document alone. But it is structurally thin against the rubric: no dedicated Target Users section (patient segments appear only inside the Problem narrative, never named with their situation as a primary/secondary split), no Functional Requirements table or MoSCoW priorities anywhere (undermines the ask's own stated goal of handing this to a build team), and the single Open Issue (EHR) is prose without a clean owner+date row rather than a real open-questions table. It also mentions all three scenario distractors (GDPR, voice-to-text, no-show speculation) even though each is dismissed - the GDPR aside in particular has no reason to appear in a disciplined document of this type, which A includes and B does not. Net: strong judgment and honesty about conflicts, but not build-ready as written.

Clearly the more scopable document: dedicated Target Users section naming primary (patients, including the 65+ segment and their situation) and secondary (front desk staff) users; a Functional Requirements table with MoSCoW priority on every row; NFR table; Dependencies table with owner+status; Open Questions table with owner and a needed-by milestone for both entries; explicit stop/pause condition in both the Risks table and the Rollout plan. All 5 probes answerable from the document alone, and it avoids the GDPR distractor entirely (unlike A), though it still surfaces voice-to-text and no-show as non-goals, which is noise the scenario doesn't want repeated even when framed as an exclusion. Minor deduction: FR-5 states EHR integration as a firm 'Must' against 'Epic' while the Open Questions/Dependencies tables simultaneously flag Epic-vs-athenahealth as unresolved and blocking - not a hard logical contradiction, but looser than A's explicit 'we're proceeding on Epic per IT, and this must be confirmed before integration work starts' framing. Unhappy-path/empty-state UX description is essentially absent (only FR-7 partially touches an error state). Solid, shippable-with-nitpicks work, not untouchable.

Rubric: problem_weight_and_evidence 4 (22-min baseline, 40% error rate, $18/resubmission, n=214 survey at 72%, 35% aged 65+; Problem plus Context out-develops the one-paragraph Solution overview). goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit 4 (goals phrased as outcomes; three non-goals each with a stated reason - kiosks/budget, voice-to-text/not scoped, no-show/no data - but goals carry no target value, only 'below baseline'). target_user_specificity 4 (primary = patients doing new-patient intake, with the 65+/35% sub-segment and its situation named, plus an explicit not-optimized-for group). metrics_primary_and_guardrail 3 (the pieces exist - intake time as primary, complaint volume as the must-not-worsen gate, first-month window - but they are scattered across Goals and Rollout, nothing is labelled primary or guardrail, and no target number is ever committed; this is the client's explicit 'how we'll know it worked' ask and it is the weakest part of the document). open_questions_owned_and_dated 4 (two rows, real owners as roles - IT director + practice administrator, practice administration - and real milestones 'before integration build begins', 'before Main St build'; no named individual in the table). unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements 2 (MoSCoW is on every FR row, which is half the criterion, but there is no UX/design section at all and no empty, loading, or error states beyond FR-7's incomplete-field flag).
Held-out: scopable 3 (FR/dependency rows are sizeable with owners and blocked/in-progress status, but three of four NFR rows are form without substance - 'HIPAA-compliant', 'available during clinic hours', and an accessibility row, 'usable by 65+ without assistance for at least basic fields', that is the crux of the design and is unsizeable as written; also never says how the pre-arrival form reaches the patient). stop_or_kill 4 (pilot gate stated twice, with threshold, first-month window, and the halt action 'expansion pauses'). no_internal_contradiction 4 (found none; the kiosk non-goal and FR-4's staff-assisted device path are reconciled explicitly in the Solution overview). decision_vs_input 4 ('per IT', 'Leadership pauses expansion if', 'This document treats October 1 as the committed target', 'lean toward patient-owned-device' all separate the received input from the author's call).
Distractors: omits GDPR entirely - the cleanest discipline of the two. Carries voice-to-text twice (Non-goals and an FR-8 'Won't' row), which pulls a hallway idea into the requirements table, and carries the no-show non-target. Probes: 5/5, all answerable from the document alone including the $16,000 gap and its proposed resolution.
Holistic 4 rather than 5: a senior practitioner would add committed metric targets, a labelled primary/guardrail pair, unhappy-path coverage, and would strike FR-8.

Rubric: problem_weight_and_evidence 4 (same evidence set, attributed - Denise Ruiz on the 22 minutes, billing on the 40%/$18, n=214 - and framed as a revenue-cycle drain rather than a complaint; Problem clearly outweighs the Scope section). goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit 4 (goal is an outcome; three out-of-scope entries each with a reason). target_user_specificity 2 (no target-users section anywhere; the 65+ cohort and front-desk staff appear only inside Problem and Scope prose, and the primary segment and its situation are never stated as such - the client asked 'who it's for' and this document does not answer it as a section). metrics_primary_and_guardrail 4 (the strongest part: an explicit measurement point 'at the Main St pilot's first-month mark', intake time under 22 minutes, complaint volume at or below baseline, illegible rate under 10% with an honest 'flag as unknown until pilot data exists' - written pre-result rather than fitted). open_questions_owned_and_dated 3 (one real open issue, EHR target, with a resolution milestone 'before integration work starts' and a quasi-owner; the other unknowns - vendor pricing for the reduced tablet count - carry neither owner nor date). unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements 1 (no functional requirements list at all, therefore no MoSCoW priorities, no NFR targets beyond 7-year retention, no UX section, no empty/loading/error states).
Held-out: scopable 2 (nothing here is sizeable at row level - 'front-desk-assisted fallback path' and 'integration with the practice's EHR' are one-line scope bullets with no owner, status, or measurable target; an engineer would need a conversation to start almost anything, though it does supply the link/QR delivery mechanism that A omits). stop_or_kill 4 (prominent, attributed 'leadership-set', hard-gate framing; nitpick - it is headed 'Rollback trigger' while the action is actually a pause on expansion, not a rollback). no_internal_contradiction 4 (no two statements that cannot both be true; the 'target under 10% but flag as unknown' line is muddled rather than contradictory). decision_vs_input 4 (its best dimension - 'Recommendation:', 'per IT, since IT owns the technical relationship', 'Note for the record', 'one team member speculated' consistently separate judgment from instruction; blemished by extending Carla Nguyen's authority to clinical-workflow input, which the brief does not support, stated in the same flat register as the sourced facts).
Distractors: the less disciplined of the two. Carries all three - and surfaces GDPR into a Compliance requirements section, which is precisely where a non-obligation does not belong, even framed as a negation. Voice-to-text appears three times (Out of scope, Risks, Decision authority). Probes: 5/5, crisply answered.
Holistic 3: better reasoning and better metrics than its structure suggests, but it is a decision memo, not the buildable artifact the brief asked to hand to whoever designs and builds the replacement - no requirements, no priorities, no target user.

Rubric: problem section (22-min figure sourced to Denise Ruiz, 40% illegible-field rate, $18/resubmission, 214-respondent survey) is both evidenced and visibly longer/heavier than the one-paragraph solution overview (5). Goals are outcome-phrased (drop below 22 min, don't raise complaints) and all three non-goals name a reason, including two that correctly fence off scenario distractors (voice-to-text, no-show) inside the legitimate Non-goals slot rather than elsewhere (5). Target users names a specific primary segment (pre-visit/at-arrival intake patients, the 72% phone-preferring cohort) plus an explicitly-not-optimized-for 65+ cohort with its own fallback need (5). Primary metric, guardrail, and a stated 30-day window are all present and pre-committed rather than fitted after the fact (5). Open questions table has two rows with named owners (IT Director, Practice Administrator) and milestone-based needed-by dates (5). Weakest rubric criterion: the FR table marks every row 'Must' (no real prioritization signal) and there is no UX section with empty/loading/error states (2) - this is a genuine content gap, not a structure nitpick, so it drags the mean down. Held-out: dependencies/FR/NFR tables with owners and statuses make most of the document scopable without a meeting, though the still-open EHR question limits full sizing (4); the rollout section names an explicit, leadership-set halt trigger tied to the guardrail metric (5); no internal contradictions found across goals/non-goals/FRs/rollout (5); the document repeatedly marks its own calls versus what it was told - 'this document treats October 1 as committed... as the newer and more specific instruction' and the same move on the Epic/athenahealth conflict (5). All 5 probes answerable from the text alone. Distractor discipline: omits GDPR entirely; names voice-to-text and no-show only inside Non-goals with a stated reason, which is the sanctioned use of that slot rather than gratuitous inclusion.

Rubric: problem section is well evidenced and adds real context (Riverside FTE gap, Oak Park's undefined process) but the 'Scope for launch' section (four in-scope bullets and three out-of-scope bullets, each with justification) is comparable in length and development to the problem section, so problem does not clearly outweigh solution as the criterion requires (3). A single overarching goal sentence is solution-flavored ('replace paper intake with a digital process that...'), with outcome-style success bullets underneath rather than a clean set of outcome goals; non-goals are present and well-reasoned (4). No dedicated Target users section exists at all - the 72%-phone / 65%-struggle tension is discussed only inside Problem and Scope, so a reader cannot point to a named primary segment with its situation the way the criterion asks (2). Success metrics are strong: primary, guardrail, and a bolded, explicitly hard-gated rollback trigger (5). Open questions has no table and only one item (EHR) gets even informal owner/timing language; the Riverside staffing compounding factor is never posed as a question needing an owner or date (2). There is no functional-requirements table and therefore no per-row MoSCoW priority, and no UX section with empty/loading/error states (1) - a real gap for a document whose own ask was to be handed to whoever builds the replacement. Held-out: with no FR/dependency table, an engineer would need a clarifying conversation to size or sequence most of the work, though the budget arithmetic is concrete enough to act on alone (2); the rollback trigger is stated at least as explicitly as Artifact A's, arguably more prominently (5); no internal contradictions found (5); decision-vs-input is well marked throughout (the Q1-supersession note, the Epic-per-IT call, the budget recommendation) (5). All 5 probes answerable from the text alone. Distractor discipline is weaker than Artifact A: it spends a dedicated Compliance bullet dismissing GDPR even though GDPR was never a live constraint, and its no-show non-goal restates the speculative 'might halve no-shows' claim in more detail than needed - both are on-topic rejections but they still spend document space on facts the ask never needed addressed at all.

Strong on decision-vs-input tracing (explicitly narrates why October 1 beats the June email, why Epic over athenahealth, why BYOD over kiosks) and states a hard rollback/kill gate tied to a metric threshold. Metrics are substantively primary+guardrail+window even though unlabeled (intake time below baseline, complaint volume at/below baseline, first-month window) - scored on substance per the anti-form rule. Weak on target-user specificity (mentions the 65+ and phone-preferring cohorts but never names a primary segment with a situation, falls back to describing 'patients' broadly), open-question ownership (the EHR conflict names a counterparty to resolve with, not an owner driving resolution, and carries no date), and requirements prioritization/unhappy paths (scope is prose bullets with no MoSCoW marks and no empty/loading/error-state coverage) - this also makes it harder to scope without a follow-up conversation. Least disciplined of the two on distractors: it includes and discusses all three (GDPR, voice-to-text, no-show), where the scenario treats inclusion itself, even to dismiss, as a discipline failure.

Full-variant structure genuinely carries content, not just form: named primary/guardrail metrics with a measurement window, a target-user section that names a segment plus situation and explicitly declines to optimize away from the 65+ cohort rather than excluding them, and an open-questions table with real owners (IT Director, Practice Administrator) and needed-by milestones. Explicit stop condition matches A's. Two of the three scenario distractors (voice-to-text, no-show) still appear as non-goals - a wash against A - but it omits the GDPR distractor entirely, the cleaner showing of the two. Held below a 5 for concrete gaps a senior reviewer would flag: every functional requirement is marked 'Must' with no differentiation or cut line if the six-week timeline slips, no empty/loading/error-state description anywhere (only one line about paper fallback on outage), and the stated goal of reducing illegible-field resubmission cost has no corresponding line in Success metrics.

Distractor standard applied to both documents: a brief exclusion-with-reason is discipline; affirmative inclusion or elaboration is the penalty. A omits GDPR entirely (the cleanest possible handling), and disposes of voice-to-text and the no-show speculation in one line each under Non-goals, with the no-show line stating outright that no data connects intake to no-shows. That is disciplined handling, not padding.

Per-criterion. problem_weight_and_evidence 4: 22-minute baseline attributed to Denise Ruiz, 40% defect rate, $18 per resubmission, n=214 survey at 72%; the Problem section is visibly more developed than the two-sentence Solution overview. Nitpick is that some evidence is split into Context, thinning Problem slightly. goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit 4: goals are outcomes (cut intake time, reduce resubmission cost), non-goals each carry a stated reason (budget, not scoped, no supporting data). target_user_specificity 4: primary is patients completing new-patient intake before or at arrival, with the 72% phone/tablet preference as the situation, plus an explicit 65+ carve-out that is served rather than excluded. metrics_primary_and_guardrail 4: named primary (average intake time below 22 min), separate named guardrail (complaint volume not above baseline), stated 30-day window, all pre-result. Held back from 5 because the primary target is merely 'below baseline' with no magnitude, which a senior practitioner would sharpen. open_questions_owned_and_dated 4: two rows, owners IT Director and Practice Administrator, needed-by milestones (before build starts, before Phase 2) rather than dates. unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements 2: a MoSCoW column exists on every FR row but every row is 'Must', which defeats the criterion's stated purpose of letting engineering see what gets cut first; and there is no UX/design section at all, so no empty, loading, or error states beyond one reliability NFR naming a paper fallback.

Held-out. scopable_without_a_meeting 3: dependency rows carry owner and status and the FRs are mostly sizable, but the NFR targets are qualitative with no measurable thresholds, and FR-5 depends on an unresolved EHR target, so at least two load-bearing rows still need a conversation. explicit_stop_or_kill_condition 4: 'If intake time or complaints exceed baseline in month one, expansion pauses per leadership's stated condition' names both the trigger and the halting action, and it is echoed as the guardrail metric. no_internal_contradiction 4: goals, non-goals, solution, and rollout cross-check cleanly; the one soft spot is a goal about resubmission cost that no success metric measures, which is a gap rather than a contradiction. decision_vs_input_traceable 4: repeatedly separates instruction from judgment ('This document treats October 1 as committed... as the newer and more specific instruction', 'specifies Epic per IT and flags the conflict', 'per leadership's stated condition').

Probes 5/5: October 1 with the June Q1 email explicitly superseded; pause condition stated in Rollout; $16,000 gap with both figures and the BYOD resolution; Carla Nguyen with the medical-director exclusion; Epic per IT with the athenahealth conflict flagged as an open dependency.

Same distractor standard. B fails it in one place and strains it in two others: it writes GDPR into its Compliance requirements section as an affirmative bullet ('No EU/GDPR obligations apply...'), which is a distractor brought into the document rather than left out; it gives voice-to-text a full paragraph under Out of scope and then a second mention under Decision authority; and it restates the no-show speculation with its origin story. Naming an exclusion is fine, but this is elaboration, and the compliance-section GDPR line is inclusion.

Per-criterion. problem_weight_and_evidence 4: the same quantified evidence, well marshalled, and the Problem is clearly the heaviest section. goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit 4: the goal is outcome-phrased and each out-of-scope item carries a reason. target_user_specificity 2: there is no target users section and no named primary segment with a situation; user groups surface only incidentally inside the Problem narrative (the 65+ cohort, 'patients'), so a reader cannot point to a primary persona. metrics_primary_and_guardrail 4: first-month window, intake time below baseline, complaint volume at or below baseline, and an illegibility target under 10% with the unknown honestly flagged; the primary-versus-guardrail roles are inferable rather than labelled. open_questions_owned_and_dated 2 (contestable, tie broken downward per protocol): the EHR open issue does carry a who and a when in prose ('resolved explicitly with the practice administrator before integration work starts'), but there is no owned open-questions structure anywhere, and the Risks and unknowns bullets carry no owners or needed-by markers at all. unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements 1: no functional requirements list, therefore no MoSCoW priorities on anything, and no empty, loading, or error states; the assisted-fallback path is the only unhappy-path gesture.

Held-out. scopable_without_a_meeting 2: there are no requirement rows, no NFR targets, and no dependency table with owner and status, so an engineer has narrative scope but nothing sizable; the tablet count and pricing are explicitly unconfirmed. explicit_stop_or_kill_condition 4: the rollback trigger is stated with its condition, its action, and its source. Not scored above A on the strength of its bolding and 'hard gate' phrasing, which is emphasis, not additional substance. no_internal_contradiction 4: no two statements conflict; the 'six weeks or less from any build kickoff' framing is loose but not contradictory. decision_vs_input_traceable 4: clearly separates told from decided ('leadership-set', 'per IT, since IT owns the technical relationship', 'Recommendation: do not close this gap by cutting scope').

Probes 5/5: all five retrievable, including the $45,000/$61,000/$16,000 arithmetic and the Epic-over-athenahealth call with its reasoning.

Full six-section-plus PRD structure with real substance in every table, not decoration: Target users names a primary segment (new patients, phone/tablet, cites the 72%/n=214 figure) and a secondary segment with a stated design constraint (65+, staff-assisted path required) - clean 5. Success metrics has a distinct primary metric, a distinct guardrail, and a measurement window stated before any result - 5. Open questions has three rows each with a named owner and a needed-by milestone tied to a phase gate - 5. Goals/non-goals: two goals are outcome-phrased but one goal is really a feature ('capture HIPAA consent and photo'), and non-goals name two exclusions with real reasons (budget math, unvalidated idea) - 4.
