Functional requirements carry MoSCoW priority on every row (partial credit for unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements) but there is no empty/loading/error-state UX description anywhere, so that criterion lands at 3. problem_weight_and_evidence is the real miss: checked word-for-word, the Problem section (~68 words) is shorter than the Solution overview section (~83 words) - the rubric's literal test ('reads as longer... not the reverse') fails, despite good evidence density, so this scores 2, not the 4-5 the rest of the document would suggest. Held-out: the pilot-gate/rollout-pause condition is explicit and tied to an action (5); no internal contradiction found across goals/non-goals/FRs/rollout (5); every FR/NFR/dependency row carries enough (owner, status, or explicit 'open, needed before X') to size without a meeting (4); decision-vs-input is present but understated - conflicts (Epic vs athenahealth, Oct 1 vs Q1, kiosk budget) are resolved and attributed ('per IT', 'superseded by') but never narrated in the author's own voice as a judgment call, so 3.5. One distractor leaks in: voice-to-text is carried into Non-goals rather than left out entirely. All 5 probes answerable correctly from the document alone, including the Carla-Nguyen authority question (though it never mentions the medical director explicitly, the core question is still answered).

Reads as a decision memo rather than a scopable PRD, and that shows up directly in the checkable criteria. problem_weight_and_evidence is the one clear win: the Problem section runs two full paragraphs with specific attributed figures and is unambiguously longer/more developed than the terse Scope section - 4. Goals are cleanly outcome-phrased (cut time, cut error rate, don't raise complaints) - 4. But there is no Target users section; the 72%/65+ figures sit inside Problem prose with no primary/secondary label or stated situation, so a reader has to infer rather than point - 3. Metrics content all exists (goals double as primary metrics, a separate Success gate section states the guardrail and a first-month window) but it is split across sections with no explicit 'primary metric' framing - 4. Open questions is an unlabeled bullet list: owners are implied in prose, not stated as a field, and there is no date/milestone beyond 'before build' - 3. There is no functional-requirements table at all, so no MoSCoW priority markers exist anywhere and no unhappy-path/error-state coverage either - 1, the low point of the document. Held-out: the halt condition is stated at least as forcefully as Artifact A's ('a hard gate, not a soft target') - 5; no internal contradiction found - 5; decision_vs_input_traceable is the standout - explicit 'Decision:' headers narrate the author's own reasoning in first person for every stakeholder conflict (timeline, EHR, hardware), which is exactly what this held-out criterion is checking for - 5; but scopable_without_a_meeting suffers for the same reason the rubric criteria do - no FR table, no NFR table, no dependency table with owner/status, so an engineer would have to extract commitments from paragraphs and would likely still need to ask what's Must vs Should - 2. Two distractors leak in, not one: voice-to-text AND the GDPR aside both get an explicit out-of-scope callout, which is less disciplined than leaving irrelevant facts out entirely. All 5 probes still answerable correctly, and probe 4 (decision authority) is answered more completely than Artifact A since it explicitly names that the medical director does not control sequencing.

Rubric breakdown: problem_weight_and_evidence=5 (Denise Ruiz's 22-min figure, the 40%/$18 resubmission math, and the 214-respondent survey give the Problem section real, named evidence, and it clearly outweighs the thin, decision-embedded solution content); goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit=3 (the three Goals are genuine outcomes, but the out-of-scope bullets mostly list items without a stated reason each - only the GDPR line gets an explicit rationale); target_user_specificity=2 (patient segments are cited inside the Problem narrative but there is no dedicated Target users section naming a primary persona and their situation); metrics_primary_and_guardrail=3 (the Success gate section states a real guardrail and a first-month window, but no metric is separately labeled 'primary' distinct from the guardrail); open_questions_owned_and_dated=2 (three open items are listed but none carries a named owner or a needed-by date, just prose pointing at 'IT and the practice administrator'); unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements=1 (no UX unhappy-path detail and no requirements table with MoSCoW priority at all). Held-out breakdown: scopable_without_a_meeting=2 (no FR/NFR/dependency rows exist to size - only prose); explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=5 (an unambiguous hard halt gate, instrumented from day one); no_internal_contradiction=5 (checked Goals against Scope and Rollout against the success gate - nothing conflicts); decision_vs_input_traceable=5, the document's clear strength - each 'Decision:' block explicitly separates what a stakeholder said from what the author concluded and why (timeline supersession, Epic-over-athenahealth reasoning, BYOD-over-kiosk math), which is exactly the kind of authored judgment this criterion rewards. All 5 probes answerable directly from the text. Distractor discipline is weak: the GDPR aside and the voice-to-text idea are both explicitly carried into the Scope section (2 of 3 distractors present), even though both are correctly marked out of scope - inclusion itself is the penalized behavior per the eval's instruction. Net: excellent decision-making transparency and a well-evidenced problem, but this reads as a decision memo rather than a build-ready PRD - missing target-user framing, dated ownership, and any prioritized requirement structure that engineering would need. Nitpick-plus-gap territory, not shippable as-is.

Rubric breakdown: problem_weight_and_evidence=4 (same core evidence as the other document - Ruiz's figure, the 40%/$18 math, the survey - carried in a Problem section that is comparable in weight to the Solution overview, though the separate Context section slightly dilutes which section is 'the' problem statement); goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit=4 (goals mix true outcomes with one feature-shaped item, but both non-goals carry an explicit stated reason - budget math for kiosks, validation status for voice-to-text); target_user_specificity=4 (a real Target users section names a primary segment doing pre-visit self-serve intake and a secondary segment with a stated tablet-friction constraint, not an undifferentiated 'all patients'); metrics_primary_and_guardrail=5 (a dedicated Success metrics section states a primary metric tied to the baselines, a separate guardrail, and an explicit first-month measurement window - textbook match to the criterion); open_questions_owned_and_dated=5 (all three open-question rows carry a named owner and a needed-by milestone, none left as TBD); unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements=3 (every FR row carries a MoSCoW-style priority, but there is no dedicated UX empty/loading/error-state treatment - only FR-6's incomplete-field flag gestures at an error path). Held-out breakdown: scopable_without_a_meeting=4 (FR, NFR, and Dependencies tables give an engineer enough to size and find blockers on most rows, though FR-5's target system is still open); explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=5 (the guardrail is restated consistently across Success metrics, Risks, and Rollout); no_internal_contradiction=5 (checked Goals/Non-goals, Target users/Solution overview, FR/NFR against Rollout - all consistent, e.g. the assisted-path NFR matches the 65+ constraint named earlier); decision_vs_input_traceable=4 (the Epic-vs-athenahealth and timeline calls are stated with their basis - 'per IT', 'superseded by more recent direction' - but with less of the author's own weighing of competing inputs than the sharpest comparator). All 5 probes answerable directly from the text. Distractor discipline is better but not clean: voice-to-text appears as a Non-goal (1 of 3 distractors present), correctly excluded but still included in the document, which the eval instructs to penalize; GDPR and the no-show claim are both absent, correctly. Net: this is a genuinely complete, buildable PRD - owners, dates, priorities, and a properly separated primary/guardrail metric are actually present, not just formatted to look present - with the one real gap being unhappy-path/UX coverage and a slightly thinner decision-rationale voice. Solid work with real nitpicks, not a 5.

Problem is evidenced (22 min per Denise Ruiz, 40% illegible/missing, $18 per resubmission, Riverside short one FTE) and runs slightly longer than the Solution overview. Goals are outcomes but unquantified - 'materially below current baselines' rather than a target number; non-goals name kiosks and voice-to-text with reasons. Target users names a primary segment (new patients completing intake on their own device before arrival, 72% of n=214) and a hard secondary constraint (65+, ~35%, needing an assisted path). Success metrics carry a primary (intake time and illegible rate vs. the 22-min/40% baselines), a separate guardrail (complaint volume), and a measurement window (first month of the Main St pilot). Open questions table has named owners (IT director, Carla Nguyen) and needed-by milestones (before build, before Phase 1, before Phase 2). Weakest rubric line by far is unhappy paths: there is no UX/design section at all, so no empty, loading, or error states - only the MoSCoW half of that criterion is met (Must/Should on every FR row). Held-out: stop condition is explicit and tied to an action (expansion pauses); no internal contradiction found - the Epic-per-IT stance is reconciled with FR-5's 'confirmed EHR system' by an open dependency rather than conflicting with it; decision-vs-input is traceable but flatter than it could be ('This PRD treats Epic as the system of record per IT', 'superseded by their more recent direction') and sources are listed in an appendix. Scopability is the soft spot: the Accessibility NFR ('usable without requiring unaided tablet use') and the unquantified goal targets are too vague to size, and the compliance dependency has a status but no date. Distractor discipline is good: GDPR and the no-show-halving claim are absent entirely; voice-to-text appears only as a reasoned non-goal, the mildest form of inclusion. All five probes answerable from this document alone.

Problem section is the document's strongest part: quantified on all three fronts, holds the 72%-prefer-digital finding against the 65+/35% staff objection, and clearly outweighs the short Scope section. Goals are three real outcomes with thresholds (below 22 minutes, below ~40%, no rise in complaints). But there is no Target users section at all - no named primary segment, persona, or the situation they are in; a reader has to infer it from the problem narrative. There are no functional requirements, so no MoSCoW priorities, and no UX section, so no empty/loading/error states - that criterion fails on both halves. 'Open items requiring resolution before build' lists three bullets that name IT and the practice administrator as parties to consult rather than as owners of the action, with no dates beyond the section header. Held-out: the stop condition is the best-executed element in either document ('hard gate, not a soft target', both metrics, first month, instrument from day one), and decision-vs-input traceability is exemplary - the three 'Decision:' sections state what was handed to the author, what the author chose, and why, and mark the EHR call as blocking. No internal contradiction: the clinic-owned tablets are consistently distinguished from the out-of-scope kiosk hardware. Scopability is where it falls down - no FR rows, no NFR targets, no dependency table with owners or status, and the hardware cost is left to a follow-up quote, so an engineer could not size or sequence this without a conversation. Distractor discipline is worse than it looks: the out-of-scope line imports GDPR and spends a clause dismissing it, and voice-to-text is listed with no reason given; the no-show claim is correctly absent. All five probes answerable, and probe 4 is answered most completely here (Carla Nguyen, with the explicit note that the medical director does not control sequencing).

Problem section (22-min baseline, 40% illegible rate, $18/resubmission, n=214 survey, 65+ struggle rate) is evidenced but runs roughly the same length as the Solution overview (which itself carries a long EHR-conflict paragraph), so the 'problem outweighs solution' check is only marginal, not clean. Target users names a specific primary segment plus a hard-constraint secondary segment (65+, ~35%) with situational detail -- strong. Goals are outcome-phrased ('cut intake time below baseline') and Non-goals give a reason each, but two Non-goals (GDPR, voice-to-text) exist only to narrate distractor facts from the brief, which the scenario explicitly penalizes even when framed as exclusions. Success metrics section is labeled Primary/Guardrail but both slots reuse the same two measures (intake time, complaint volume) rather than a primary tied to a goal plus a distinct guardrail -- structurally present but conceptually muddled. Open questions has two rows with named owners and 'before build'/'before pilot launch' milestones -- real, not placeholder. Full-variant coverage is genuinely present: FR table carries Must/Should on every row, and UX and design names an edge case (patient shows up without completing intake) and an error case (illegible card photo) distinct from the happy path. Stop condition is explicit and unambiguous (guardrail pause on regression). Decisions (EHR, budget, timeline) are narrated as settled facts more than as 'I decided X over Y because Z' -- traceable but less explicit in authorial voice than a document that names the decision act itself. Answered all 5 probes correctly and specifically, including the EHR conflict resolution and the $16k budget gap math.

Problem section is the strongest of the two on evidence-and-weight: named source (front desk manager Denise Ruiz), the same quantified costs, and explicit synthesis of the conflicting survey/staff signals ('Both are true and both matter'), running clearly longer and more developed than the terse two-paragraph Scope section it sits against. But the document is missing structural pieces the rubric explicitly checks for: there is no Target users section at all (segments appear only embedded in Problem/Scope prose, not named as a persona with a situation), no Functional requirements table (so no MoSCoW priority anywhere), and no UX and design section (no empty/loading/error states named). Open items is an unowned, undated bullet list -- only the EHR item names who to confirm with; the other two have neither owner nor a needed-by date, so it reads as a to-do note rather than an owned table. This also weakens scopable_without_a_meeting: with no FR rows, no NFR targets, and no dependency table, an engineer has decisions and rationale to read but no sized, blocker-tagged work items to estimate from. Where it clearly leads is decision_vs_input_traceable: three explicit 'Decision:' sections each state what was told (the ops director's June email vs. the later meeting; IT's 'Epic' vs. the practice administrator's 'athenahealth') and what the author chose and why, in first-person reasoning -- the clearest authorship-vs-input separation of the two. The stop/kill condition is stated with equal force to A ('a hard gate, not a soft target'). Like A, it narrates two of the three distractor facts (GDPR, voice-to-text) as out-of-scope items rather than omitting them outright. Answered all 5 probes correctly and precisely, including an explicit statement that the medical director does not control rollout sequencing.

Rubric scores: problem_weight_and_evidence 4 (named source Denise Ruiz, quantified $18/claim, n=214 survey; Problem section is comparable in length to the combined 'Decision' sections but there is no single 'Solution overview' heading to check against literally), goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit 4 (three outcome-phrased goals; only the GDPR out-of-scope line carries an explicit stated reason, the other two out-of-scope items rely on the reader connecting earlier sections), target_user_specificity 2 (no dedicated Target users section; elderly subsegment is mentioned only inside Problem, no named primary persona with situation), metrics_primary_and_guardrail 3 (has a measurable target and a first-month window, but does not label one metric primary and one guardrail - the gate section treats both as a single combined trigger), open_questions_owned_and_dated 2 (three bullets, no owner column, no per-item date, only a shared 'before build' milestone), unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements 1 (no FR table, no priority markers, no UX/error-state section at all). Held-out: scopable_without_a_meeting 2 (zero FR/NFR/dependency rows exist to point to - fails the check structurally even though prose carries some sizing-relevant facts), explicit_stop_or_kill_condition 5 (explicit hard gate on intake time and complaint volume, first month, named consequence), no_internal_contradiction 5 (checked Goals vs Non-goals/Scope, Decision sections vs Rollout, found no conflicting statements), decision_vs_input_traceable 5 (this is the document's clear strength: each 'Decision:' section explicitly names the conflicting inputs - June email vs. meeting statement, IT vs. practice-administrator email - and states in first person which one the author is going with and why, e.g. 'I'm going with Epic, per IT, because IT owns the technical integration'). All 5 probes answerable from the document alone. Holistic 3: the reasoning and conflict-resolution content is genuinely strong, but as a document meant to be handed to whoever designs and builds the replacement, it is missing structural pieces (target users, prioritized FRs, unhappy-path UX, dated/owned open questions) that a senior practitioner would flag as real gaps, not nitpicks - this is a decision memo more than a build-ready PRD. Includes 2 of 3 distractors (GDPR, voice-to-text, both listed as out-of-scope items) - does not include the no-show claim.

Rubric scores: problem_weight_and_evidence 3 (quantified evidence present but no named source for the 22-minute figure, and by literal section-to-section word count the 'Problem' heading is roughly equal to or slightly shorter than 'Solution overview', not clearly longer as the criterion asks - the stronger problem case is split across a separate 'Context and background' section instead), goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit 5 (explicit Non-goals heading with a stated reason inline for each of three items), target_user_specificity 5 (explicit Target users section naming primary and secondary segments with their situations), metrics_primary_and_guardrail 5 (explicit Primary/Guardrail/Measurement-window labels, directly pointable), open_questions_owned_and_dated 5 (table with populated Owner and Needed-by columns, not placeholders), unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements 4 (FR table has a Must/Should priority column on every row; UX section covers happy/assisted/edge/error cases but does not separately label an empty or loading state). Held-out: scopable_without_a_meeting 4 (FR/NFR/Dependencies tables exist with real rows; remaining unknowns, like the EHR system, are honestly flagged as open rather than silently assumed), explicit_stop_or_kill_condition 5 (guardrail breach explicitly halts expansion, stated in both Success metrics and Rollout plan), no_internal_contradiction 5 (checked Goals/Non-goals, FR-7 vs Rollout phases, Solution overview's 'working assumption' hedge vs Open questions - no two statements found that can't both be true), decision_vs_input_traceable 3 (the document resolves each conflict - flu-season date over the June email, Epic over athenahealth, BYOD over kiosk budget - but reports the resolution in flat declarative voice rather than attributing it to the author's own judgment; the Epic call is hedged as a 'working assumption' needing confirmation but never given a stated reason for why Epic beats athenahealth, and the BYOD scope cut is stated as settled fact rather than marked as a call). All 5 probes answerable from the document alone. Holistic 4: solid, shippable-with-a-nitpick PRD - the rubric gap over the other artifact is grounded in named, pointable content (labeled primary/guardrail metrics, owner+date rows, a MoSCoW column, a named target-user section) rather than in headings or tone, so this is not a case of rewarding form over substance. Includes the same 2 of 3 distractors as the other artifact (GDPR, voice-to-text, both as Non-goals with reasons) - does not include the no-show claim; since both artifacts carry identical distractor exposure it does not change the relative ordering, though it is worth flagging that the rubric's own non-goals criterion rewards exactly the move the distractor rule penalizes.

Problem carries the specific evidence (22-min intake, ~40% illegible/missing rate, ~$18 per resubmission, n=214 survey with 72%, 65+ at ~35%) and out-weighs the short Solution overview. Names a primary user segment with the situation they are in (new patients completing pre-visit intake on their own device) plus a secondary 65+ segment treated as a hard design constraint, which is the single clearest content advantage over B. Goals include real outcome goals, though one is a launch date; non-goals give reasons, but two of the three (GDPR, voice-to-text) are scenario distractors rather than real scope decisions, so that section would get touched. Success metrics name intake time against the 22-minute baseline, a guardrail tied to an explicit expansion pause, and a first-month window; complaint volume is muddled by appearing as both primary and guardrail. Open questions carry named owners (IT director, practice administrator) and needed-by milestones, and dependencies carry owner and status. Unhappy paths are partial: happy, assisted, edge, and error cases are described but no empty or loading states; FR table does carry Must/Should priorities. Held-out: scopable is limited by an NFR row with no measurable target (accessibility is stated as prose, not a threshold) and by tablet count being unknown; stop condition is explicit and stated twice consistently; no internal contradiction found, with the Epic-vs-athenahealth tension explicitly reconciled as a working assumption; decision-vs-input is the weakest held-out dimension, since several load-bearing calls (the kiosk scope cut, the BYOD choice) are reported flat so a reader cannot tell whether the author decided or was told. Distractors: GDPR and voice-to-text both appear, as explicit exclusions with reasons; the unsupported no-show-halving claim is correctly absent.
